pass_b_english: Those who are numb in mind are burdened as if with a heart, but if someone examines the Gentiles closely, they will find them to be such and no different, for they were raised through faith and became children of Abraham, and fellow heirs of Isaac, and sharers in the blessing on him.
Paul will testify to this, saying that the Scripture foretold that God justifies the Gentiles through faith, and that all nations will be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3, 22:18).
The one who came from Abraham, Isaac, is formed into our Lord Jesus Christ (Genesis 22:2), and it can be shown from all sides, and very easily.

The promise to Abraham is fulfilled again in those who believe in Christ, and Paul will assure us of this, writing to the Galatians that no one annuls or adds to a ratified human covenant, but the promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed, and he does not say seeds as if many, but as one, and to his seed who is Christ (Galatians 3:16).
As many as were baptized into Christ put on Christ, and there is no distinction between Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female, for you are all one in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:27-28).
Therefore, you are the descendants of Abraham and heirs according to the promise.
The multitude of things said provides sufficient proof for the subject at hand.
However, if you think I have spoken too little, O Jew, and that my words are of no value, and you refuse to agree with us, then the blame lies not with me, but with your disobedience.

Those who strive to speak the most powerful words cannot be held responsible if they fail to persuade their listeners, for they have worked diligently to express what is within them, and thus they are free from blame.

On the other hand, those who listen to the best teachings and yet refuse to agree are guilty of the most shameful behavior, similar to one who receives a loan and proves to be ungrateful and ignorant, for such a person does not demonstrate the lender's evil, but rather their own.
By considering the experiences of doctors, I realize that their pursuit of the medical art is wise, and their discoveries about the sick are not outside the realm of sober reasoning.

Let us, therefore, imitate their approach and treat the stubborn with the same remedies, so to speak, for just as doctors restore the health of one who has fallen into sickness, if they see that the passions have taken you, they present a variety of restraints and order you to take what is sufficient from all sides, doing well.

The Jewish person, who has much foolishness as a disease, is invited to obey and follow the path of righteousness, and by looking at the story of Isaac, we can see a prefiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Abraham, the renowned patriarch, was given a command by God that seemed harsh and paradoxical to some: to sacrifice his beloved son Isaac as a whole burnt offering (Genesis 22:2).
This command raises questions about the nature of God and the morality of such an action, for how could God advise Abraham to kill his own son, who was righteous and barely given to him in old age?

The patriarch's response to this command teaches us about the importance of obedience and trust in God's plan, for by silencing our own doubts and establishing a household management based on the announced, we can learn to trust in God's wisdom and vote against the inhumanity that can arise from our own foolishness.

God's commands are not meant to be harsh or inhumane, but rather to test our faith and trust in Him, as evident in the story of Abraham and Isaac, where God says, 'Take your beloved son, whom you loved, Isaac, and go to the high land and offer him as a whole burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will tell you' (Genesis 22:2).

Abraham, not neglecting the divine command, considered it more important than his affection for his child and obeyed, taking his son Isaac to the place God had told him, and after cutting wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place God had told him, on the third day.

From afar, Abraham saw the place and said to his servants, showing his trust in God's command, 'Sit with the donkey, I and the child will go as far as here, and having worshiped, we will return to you.', and then he took the wood for the burnt offering and put it on his son Isaac, and he also took the fire and the knife.

The two of them went together to the place that God had told him, where Abraham built an altar and arranged the wood on it, and then he bound Isaac and put him on the altar on top of the wood, stretching out his hand to take the knife and slaughter his son.

Just as Abraham was about to sacrifice Isaac, an angel of the Lord called out to him, saying 'Abraham, Abraham' (Genesis 22:11), and Abraham replied, 'Here I am.', and the angel then instructed him not to lay a hand on the child or do anything to him, saying 'Now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld your beloved son from me.', and Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in a thorn bush, which he then took and offered as a burnt offering instead of his son Isaac, thus fulfilling the divine command without sacrificing his child.

On the third day, he comes, having ordered two servants to follow him, and the fact that the child is carried to the sacrifice by the father symbolizes that it was not human power or the plotting of those who sought to harm him that led Jesus Christ to the cross, but rather the will of the Father, who allowed him to endure death for the sake of all.

The Savior also spoke to Pilate, saying that he had no authority over him unless it was given from above (John 19:11), and to the Father in heaven, saying, 'Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me, yet not as I will, but as you will' (Matthew 26:42)...
